input.task_description:
Regression of the near-core rotation frequency of a pulsating star from a
single TESS light curve.

Each sample is one star observed in one TESS sector: a univariate sequence
of normalized brightness measurements. The target is frot, the star's
near-core rotation frequency in cycles per day. The population is the
GDOR_SPB class of the PhyTS TESS benchmark — intermediate- and high-mass
g-mode pulsators — for which a rotation frequency could be derived.

The physical signal is periodic: rotation shifts the frequencies of the
star's gravity-mode pulsations, so the information lives in the sequence's
periodic structure rather than in its amplitude. Each curve is z-scored
individually before the model sees it, which removes absolute brightness
and per-star scale; what survives is the shape of the variability.

What makes this hard. Sampling is uneven in a way the fixed-length tensor
does not show: the released curves were taken at two different cadences
(30-minute and 10-minute), so a fixed 1024-sample window covers a
different physical duration depending on which mission observed the star,
and the frequency content is not aligned across samples. Targets span
roughly -0.27 to 17.45 cycles per day but concentrate near 1, so a model
that predicts the mean is not obviously wrong and scores exactly 0.0.

Two properties of the labels are worth knowing because they bound what is
achievable. First, frot is derived per LIGHT CURVE, not per star, so the
same star observed in different sectors can carry different target values;
if a model predicted each star's mean target perfectly it would score
R-squared 0.92 on train and 0.98 on validation, which is the label-noise
ceiling. Second, 26 of 4,183 released rows carry a negative frot, 23 of
them the exact repeated constant -0.271916. That value is almost certainly
a pipeline sentinel rather than 23 independent measurements; it is
retained unfiltered because the task definition is the released data, but
a model is not expected to reproduce it.

Published reference points. These are the benchmark's own numbers, known
to anyone who reads it, and they describe the task rather than recommend
an approach. All were computed on a TEST split while a run here is scored
on VALIDATION, and R-squared is normalized by the evaluation set's own
variance, so they are not a target to beat on the same footing.

  supervised baselines, all at 300K parameters:
    S4D                 R-squared 0.665   diagonal state-space model
    CNN                 R-squared 0.617   described only as a vanilla CNN
    LinOSS              R-squared 0.612   oscillatory state-space model
    mean predictor      R-squared -0.017  predicts the training mean

  the same three across a capacity sweep (~10k / ~100k / ~300k / ~700k),
  each cell the top-3 mean of a 100-iteration hyperparameter sweep:
    LinOSS   0.536 / 0.589 / 0.612 / 0.598
    S4D      0.581 / 0.624 / 0.665 / 0.522
    CNN      0.573 / 0.580 / 0.617 / 0.591

  six pretrained time-series foundation models, zero-shot, on the paper's
  own re-split rather than this one: 0.074 to 0.305, with the strongest
  being Chronos at 0.3049 and MOMENT at 0.2631. Fine-tuning raises the
  best of them to 0.4095.

Baseline architectures, read from the benchmark's code repository rather
than the paper, which publishes only family names:

  CNN     five blocks of Conv1d(kernel 15, same padding) -> BatchNorm1d
          -> GELU -> MaxPool1d(2) -> Dropout(0.4), channels
          64/64/128/128/256, then a global average pool over time and one
          Linear to the output. An optional validity mask multiplies the
          input first.
  S4D     Linear encoder to d_model 64, then 4 residual blocks of
          S4D(d_state 16, dt 0.001-0.1) -> dropout 0.2 -> residual add
          -> LayerNorm, then a mask-aware mean pool over time and one
          Linear to the output.
  LinOSS  4 blocks, each a BatchNorm, an oscillatory state-space layer
          with diagonal A/B/C/D and learnable step sizes, a GLU, dropout
          and a residual connection. ssm_size 100, H 200, IM
          discretization.

All three pool over the whole sequence and then read a single linear head,
and all three are mask-aware or made so, which is what lets them handle the
padded tail.

Three things about those published numbers do not line up, and are worth
knowing before treating any of them as a target. The committed configs
measure far larger than the 300K the paper reports: the CNN config counts
926,536 parameters and the LinOSS config's own comment targets S4D near
662K, which places them at the sweep's ~700k point rather than the ~300k
point the headline results come from, and at ~700k the sweep shows S4D
falling to 0.522. The committed configs also use a 70/15/15 split rather
than the released 80/10/10 one used here. And the repository commits no
regression config for TESS at all, only a classification one.

The full record, including the foundation-model architectures, the
published training setup and the exact discrepancies above, is in
`declared/reference_baselines.json`.

NOTE: This implementation passes trainability checks but deviates from the proposed mathematical spec. The tuner is optimizing an approximation of the intended architecture. Deviations: The model has valid tensor shapes, differentiable trainable paths through the cadence gate, encoder, and regression head, and emits the declared [B, 1] regressor output. Fidelity is not exact because constant-tail detection uses a 1e-6 tolerance rather than exact equality, and the expected cadence and duration scalars are normalized before concatenation rather than used directly as mathematically defined.

Focus areas: First verify that constant-tail mask extraction recovers plausible valid lengths; tune padding_tolerance and minimum trailing-run length before changing encoder capacity.; Tune cadence-gate inputs and entropy regularization, and inspect whether its posterior separates the two cadence populations rather than correlating spuriously with frot.; Tune the shared-grid resolution, upper frequency bound, Hann power normalization, and residual dilation schedule before increasing channel count.; Tune Smooth L1 beta and learning rate for robustness to rare extreme targets and the repeated negative sentinel.; Compare posterior-weighted two-hypothesis features against hard cadence assignment only if reliable cadence labels or a deterministic cadence rule become available.
Constraints: Keep predicted peak VRAM at or below 6.4 GB, which is 80% of the 8.00 GB effective cap; reduce batch size before reducing the shared spectral grid.; Do not exceed the memo's 500000-trainable-parameter ceiling without evidence from a capacity sweep; the baseline is approximately 119000 parameters.; The final layer must remain Linear(features,1) with no ReLU, sigmoid, clipping, or other output squashing.; All pooling and preprocessing must exclude the detected constant padding tail.
Known failures: Cadence is not supplied by the forward contract, so an inaccurate learned cadence posterior can map peaks onto the wrong cycles-per-day axis.; Power-only spectra discard phase and time-localized amplitude modulation that may help identify pulsation modes.; The shorter physical baseline of a 10-minute, 1024-sample window intrinsically has poorer frequency resolution; interpolation cannot restore missing resolution.; Rare extreme targets and the repeated negative sentinel can still influence optimization even with Smooth L1.; Exact or near-exact naturally constant observations at the end of a real curve may be mistaken for padding if mask tolerance is too loose.
Suggested directions: Run the baseline unchanged and record validation R-squared, cadence-posterior histograms, inferred valid-length distributions, and error stratified by inferred cadence.; Use an ablation replacing physical-frequency interpolation with sample-index spectra; a clear score drop would support the cadence-alignment hypothesis.; Use a second ablation with only one cadence hypothesis to determine whether the dual-hypothesis gate is necessary under the input-only contract.; If the result is at or below the memo's 0.35 refutation threshold, next test a hybrid spectral and time-domain branch rather than simply enlarging the spectral encoder.; Search preprocessing and Smooth L1 beta first, dilation and channels second, and batch size or dropout last.
Rationale: The model is small enough that representation correctness, especially padding removal and physical-frequency alignment, is more likely to dominate capacity. Diagnostics and ablations therefore target the causal mechanism directly, while the tuning order avoids spending trials on larger encoders before establishing that cadence inference and aligned spectra are informative.
memory.hypothesis: The unchanged approximately 119000-parameter baseline will train stably without collapse and provide a finite validation R-squared reference; if it is at or below 0.35, the final round should prioritize representation changes rather than increased capacity.

memory.hypothesis: The unchanged baseline with batch size 32 and full snapshot scope will provide enough stable timing observations to pass runtime admission, complete within the five-minute budget, and produce the first finite validation R-squared reference without model collapse.
memory.conclusion: Good as the first valid reference and therefore the new best by default: the run completed 100 epochs in 197.9 seconds, within the 300-second budget, produced a finite R2 of 0.759461, passed the dispersion gate, and was non-degenerate. With no prior baseline or best score, it establishes rather than beats a comparative benchmark.
memory.key_factor: The unchanged spectral ResNet configuration using smooth-L1 loss, batch size 32, and full-data scope (trial_portion 1.0) provided stable optimization and runtime; because this is the first scored run, no individual hyperparameter can yet be credited through comparison.
memory.discovery: This 117,027-parameter configuration is runtime-feasible and does not collapse: training smooth-L1 fell from 0.2282 to 0.0367, while validation fell from 0.1183 to 0.0639 and reached its best value of 0.0607 at epoch 95, drifting only about 0.0032 afterward. The final validation-training gap of about 0.0272 shows that further training gains were not fully mirrored on validation, making best-validation checkpointing preferable to automatically using the last epoch.
memory.memory_update: Adopt R2=0.759461 as the baseline score for subsequent comparisons and retain the current full-data, batch-32, smooth-L1 setup as the control. In the next run, select the best-validation checkpoint around epoch 95 and vary only one factor at a time, such as learning rate or epoch cap; do not change the loss based on this run because smooth-L1 optimization was stable and there is no same-loss competitor yet.

memory.hypothesis: The proven baseline configuration will remain stable under formal evaluation and achieve a comparable R-squared near 0.76, with only minor split-related variation and no prediction collapse.
memory.conclusion: Bad relative to the only prior best: R2=0.7131 is 0.0463 lower (6.1% relative) than 0.7595, so the hypothesis of performance near 0.76 was not validated. memory.key_factor: The executed cadence-aligned spectral ResNet configuration with smooth-L1 loss and the governed 40-epoch setting generalized worse than the previous best despite achieving a lower same-loss training objective; no supported hyperparameter improvement explains the score gain because there was none.

memory.memory_update: Retain the previous 0.7595 configuration as best and do not optimize further solely for lower smooth-L1 loss. arguments.description:
# CadenceAlignedSpectralResnet

## Overview

A compact cadence-aware spectral regressor that extracts the valid, non-padded portion of each light curve, applies a Hann window, computes log-power RFFT features, and maps them onto a common physical-frequency grid under the two possible TESS cadence hypotheses. A lightweight gate estimates the cadence from input-derived validity and variation statistics because the forward contract provides no explicit cadence metadata. The two cadence-conditioned spectra are processed by a shared residual dilated Conv1d encoder with a physical-frequency coordinate channel. Cadence-weighted spectral mean and max summaries are concatenated with inferred cadence and physical-duration scalars, passed through a small MLP, and mapped by an unsquashed Linear head to one continuous rotation-frequency prediction.

**Forward contract:** `[B, 1, 1024] float32 → [B, 1] float32` (regressor)

## Architecture

For each input x, identify the maximal constant-valued right tail and construct a validity mask m that retains its first value as the final observation while excluding subsequent padding. Let n be the valid length, center the valid samples, and multiply them by a Hann window. Compute the one-sided Fourier transform and normalized power P=|RFFT(x_valid multiplied by Hann)|^2/E_Hann, followed by log(1+P). For each candidate cadence delta in the supported cadence set, assign every Fourier coefficient the physical frequency f_k=k/(n delta), then linearly interpolate log-power onto a shared physical-frequency grid to obtain S_delta and a spectral-support mask. Estimate a cadence posterior p_delta with a small softmax gate using input-derived features such as valid fraction, padding fraction, and normalized adjacent-difference energy. Append the normalized physical-frequency coordinate to each S_delta and process every cadence hypothesis with the same encoder. Each residual encoder block computes h_next=h+PointwiseConv(Dropout(GELU(Norm(DilatedConv(Norm(h)))))); dilation increases by block while convolution is noncausal because frequency has no causal ordering. Apply support-mask-aware mean and max pooling to each encoded spectrum and combine the summaries by the cadence posterior. Concatenate this representation with the posterior expected cadence and expected physical duration n times delta. Pass the result through a GELU MLP and a final Linear(features,1), without output activation, yielding a float32 tensor of shape [B,1].

## Baseline Configuration

{
  "model_config": {
    "input_channels": 1,
    "input_length": 1024,
    "output_dim": 1,
    "cadence_minutes": [
      10.0,
      30.0
    ],
    "cadence_handling": "learned_two_hypothesis_gate",
    "cadence_gate_features": [
      "valid_fraction",
      "padding_fraction",
      "normalized_adjacent_difference_energy"
    ],
    "cadence_gate_hidden_dim": 16,
    "cadence_gate_temperature": 1.0,
    "mask_extraction": "terminal_constant_run",
    "padding_tolerance": 1e-06,
    "minimum_padding_run": 2,
    "retain_first_tail_value_as_observed": true,
    "window_type": "hann",
    "remove_valid_mean": true,
    "power_normalization": "hann_energy",
    "spectral_transform": "log1p_rfft_power",
    "frequency_grid_min_cpd": 0.0,
    "frequency_grid_max_cpd": 24.0,
    "frequency_grid_bins": 512,
    "frequency_interpolation": "linear",
    "frequency_coordinate_channel": true,
    "spectral_channels": 64,
    "residual_blocks": 4,
    "kernel_size": 5,
    "dilations": [
      1,
      2,
      4,
      8
    ],
    "causal_convolution": false,
    "normalization": "group_norm",
    "activation": "gelu",
    "dropout": 0.1,
    "skip_connection": true,
    "shared_encoder_across_cadence_hypotheses": true,
    "spectral_pooling": [
      "mask_aware_mean",
      "mask_aware_max"
    ],
    "metadata_scalars": [
      "posterior_expected_cadence",
      "posterior_expected_physical_duration"
    ],
    "mlp_hidden_dim": 128,
    "mlp_activation": "gelu",
    "mlp_dropout": 0.1,
    "head_type": "linear",
    "head_output_dim": 1,
    "head_activation": null,
    "parameter_ceiling": 500000,
    "peak_vram_target_gb": 6.4
  },
  "train_config": {
    "lr": 0.0003,
    "epochs": 40,
    "batch_size": 32,
    "optimizer_type": "adamw",
    "weight_decay": 1e-05,
    "device": "cuda"
  },
  "loss_config": {
    "loss_type": "smooth_l1",
    "beta": 0.5,
    "reduction": "mean"
  }
}
